title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest leans into fresh 2025–2026 human data: a new randomized trial on urolithin A and immune aging, updated HIIT meta-analyses for women, a pelvic-floor trial pairing e-stim with training, why TP53 status matters in HER2+ breast cancer (and where vitamin D fits), and the AASM's latest word on treating stubborn insomnia. Sources from Nature Aging, JAMA Network Open, PubMed/Europe PMC, MDPI, and the AASM are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — talk to a clinician before acting on anything here.

sections.body:
The strongest new signals this cycle come from **mitophagy activators** and **intermittent rapamycin** — both with *human* randomized data, and both with realistic, modest effect sizes.

- **Urolithin A & immune aging (new RCT).** A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in *Nature Aging* (50 healthy adults 45–70, **1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks**) found urolithin A expanded **naive-like, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells**, boosted mitochondrial biogenesis and fatty-acid oxidation in T cells, and improved monocyte function — a cellular counter to "inflammaging." Short-term and mechanistic, but a clean positive signal for a widely available (GRAS) supplement.
- **Urolithin A goes to the NIH.** An NIA-sponsored trial (**NCT06274749**) testing urolithin A on **glucose metabolism** in adults ≥55 is set to begin recruiting **Aug 26, 2026** — worth watching for metabolic (not just muscle/immune) endpoints.
- **Rapamycin, one-year human data.** The decentralized **PEARL** RCT (48 weeks, 5 or 10 mg/week compounded rapamycin vs placebo) reported **no increase in serious adverse events** and **sex-specific** benefits — the most robust being **gains in lean tissue mass in women on 10 mg/week**, plus improvements in pain, social functioning, and quality of life. Off-label use still isn't guideline-endorsed; treat as experimental.

Practical framing: favor interventions with human RCTs, expect **incremental** effects, and be wary of single-compound "longevity" claims.

sections.body:
Recent meta-analyses reaffirm HIIT as a **time-efficient** way to improve fitness and body composition in women — while nudging you to judge success by **body-fat and recomposition**, not the scale.

- **Recreationally active women.** A 2025 systematic review & meta-analysis in *Scientific Reports* (15 studies, 304 women) found significant gains in **VO2max/VO2peak** and a meaningful drop in **body-fat percentage** — but **no significant change in total body mass or fat mass**. Expect recomposition over weight loss.
- **Where HIIT ranks.** A 2025 network meta-analysis (44 RCTs, ~2,384 women) put vigorous aerobic exercise and **HIIT at the top for reducing body-fat percentage**, reinforcing that the shared ingredient — **high-intensity stimulus** — drives adiposity change.
- **Postmenopausal women.** A 12-week RCT (3×/week) found **HIIT and concurrent training** both cut weight, BMI, and abdominal fat and improved lipids and **HOMA-IR**; the concurrent (aerobic + resistance) arm edged out HIIT on body composition.
- **Dialing it in.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* review suggests **running-based** HIIT trends better than cycling for fat loss, with ≥3 sessions/week and ≥8–12 weeks for body-fat change.

Bottom line: keep the intensity high, **add resistance training**, progress volume gradually, and protect recovery.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). New 2026 trials focus on *what to add* when muscles are very weak, and *how to make training accessible*.

- **Add e-stim when the floor is very weak.** A 2026 multicentre, double-blind RCT (*Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol*) added **sEMG-triggered intravaginal electrical stimulation** to supervised PFMT in women with SUI and very weak muscles. The combo produced **earlier, greater, and longer-lasting** gains: at 12 months, +0.59 Oxford strength points, **−1.5 leakage episodes/week**, less pad use, and clinically meaningful improvement in **65% vs 18%** of controls.
- **Prevention in new mothers.** A JAMA Network Open RCT (764 primiparous women, PEFLOW program from 28 weeks' gestation) cut **SUI at 6 weeks postpartum to 8.7% vs 13.9%** and roughly doubled the share reaching strong muscle grades (MOS ≥4).
- **Before surgery.** A 2026 *Int Urogynecol J* RCT of intensive **preoperative** PFMT improved strength and symptom severity so much that **43% of women postponed** their planned sling surgery.
- **Access matters.** A telehealth PFMT RCT significantly reduced SUI severity vs education alone — useful when in-person pelvic-floor PT isn't available.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat raw reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised programs generally outperform unsupervised ones.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard HER2-targeted therapy** — not a substitute for it. Two themes stand out, plus a note on why **TP53/p53** status matters.

- **Why TP53 matters here.** A molecular-landscape study (*Cancer Medicine*) found **TP53 mutations blunt the efficacy of anti-HER2 *antibodies* (e.g., trastuzumab) but not HER2 *tyrosine-kinase inhibitors***, suggesting antibody + TKI combinations may help. SABCS 2024 data likewise linked **TP53 (found in ~53% of metastatic HER2+)** and TP53+PIK3CA co-mutations to worse progression-free survival. Germline TP53 also drives early-onset disease — genetics are worth discussing with your oncology team.
- **Correct vitamin D deficiency.** A 2026 retrospective interventional study (*Nutrients*) of curative-intent HER2+ patients found **failing to correct** a vitamin D deficiency carried a **~1.7× higher recurrence hazard**, with better disease-free survival trends at higher levels (>50 ng/mL). Two 2025 RCTs reported a **doubling of pathologic complete response** with repletion, strongest in HER2+ and triple-negative subtypes.
- **Supplements: mechanism ≠ proof.** Despite promising lab data on **curcumin** modulating HER2/NF-κB pathways, a randomized placebo-controlled trial of IV curcumin + paclitaxel (**NCT03072992**) illustrates that **clinical efficacy remains unproven**, and bioavailability and drug-interaction concerns are real.

Important framing: much of this is **early or observational**. Use integrative options as *add-ons coordinated with an oncologist* — never as replacements for HER2-targeted therapy.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or fragmented sleep, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I is still first-line.** The AASM's 2026 clinical practice guideline on *combination* treatment issued two conditional recommendations: **CBT-I + medication beats medication alone** (better global insomnia severity and sleep continuity), but **combination is *not* recommended over CBT-I alone** — CBT-I by itself delivers durable gains without drug risks. No single drug/class emerged as a preferred add-on; benefits of adding medication were **small and outcome-specific** (mainly early total-sleep-time).
- **Supplements, honestly.** The AASM continues to **suggest against melatonin, valerian, and tryptophan** for chronic insomnia due to insufficient efficacy evidence. Melatonin is best reserved for **circadian problems** (jet lag, shift work), not maintenance insomnia.
- **If medication is needed**, newer **dual orexin receptor antagonists** (e.g., lemborexant, daridorexant) are FDA-approved options often better tolerated than older hypnotics; use the **shortest effective duration** and decide via shared decision-making.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If fragmented sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
